conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to make sure you’re getting the support you deserve after having your baby.  

Today I’ll be using the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—we usually just call it the **EPDS**. It’s a short, 10-question check-in that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days.  

There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays confidential within our care team. My goal is simply to create a safe, judgment-free space where you can be honest about the joys and the hard parts of new motherhood.  

We’ll take it one question at a time; it usually only takes a few minutes. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.

So, to start:  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult for you?

I can laugh sometimes, but mostly it feels kind of forced. When my partner or a friend says something funny I’ll smile, yet it’s like the joy doesn’t really land. I don’t feel that light, easy laughter I used to have—like I’m too tired or heavy inside to fully enjoy the joke.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

No, that doesn’t sound right. I mean, I can still laugh every now and then—like if my husband pulls a silly face—but most of the time it feels kind of fake or far away. The funny side of things just doesn’t reach me the way it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Honestly, not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just watching a show I liked—but lately it all feels kind of pointless. I still do some of those things because I know I should, but the spark isn’t there. It’s like I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding him the way he needs. When he wouldn’t settle during the night, I kept replaying every little choice I made, sure it was my fault. I know, logically, babies just cry sometimes, but I still feel like I’m failing him.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. Even when everything looks fine—he’s sleeping, the house is quiet—I’ll suddenly feel this wave of worry. I keep checking if he’s breathing, if the room temperature is okay, if I sterilized the bottles right. There’s this constant tightness in my chest like something bad is about to happen, even when I can’t name what it is.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like the anxiety bubbles over and I get this rush of fear out of nowhere. My heart starts racing, my hands get clammy, and I feel like I have to check on the baby *right now* or something awful will happen. It passes after a few minutes, but those moments leave me shaky and exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the minute I finish one feeding, the next is due, the laundry’s piled up, the dishes are everywhere, and I can’t remember if I’ve eaten. I keep thinking, “How does anyone do this?” I’m not falling apart, but it’s like I’m barely treading water—constantly behind and overwhelmed.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my mind just keeps circling—did I burp him long enough, am I producing enough milk, what if he stops breathing in the night? Some nights I drift off, then jolt awake for no clear reason and can’t settle again. Even when the baby’s sleeping a decent stretch, I’m staring at the ceiling, too keyed-up or sad to rest.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time, yeah. I’ll be feeding the baby or just sitting on the couch and this heavy sadness rolls in. Everything feels gray—like I’m stuck under a cloud that won’t lift. I keep telling myself I should be happy because I have this healthy baby, but the miserable feeling just sits there anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened three, maybe four times this week. Yesterday I just looked at the pile of unfolded laundry and started sobbing. It feels like the tears come out of nowhere—one second I’m fine, the next I’m crying over something small or nothing at all.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of my baby.

You've shared that over the past week most moments feel gray and heavy: laughter rarely feels real, activities you used to anticipate now seem pointless, and you constantly question whether you're doing motherhood "right." Waves of <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic</sym> arrive uninvited, leaving your chest tight and your sleep fractured by racing thoughts about the baby's safety. You cry easily, feel overwhelmed by everyday tasks, yet you remain clear that you want to feel better and have never considered harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to laugh and find humor, with laughter feeling "fake or far away," aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports loss of anticipatory pleasure in all activities, doing them only out of obligation with no enjoyment—semantic match to "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame for normal infant behavior, indicating this happens "most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, unprovoked anxiety occurring "pretty much all the time" with physical tension and intrusive safety-checking behaviors, aligning with "Yes, very often".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms and compulsive checking on baby, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to keep up with basic tasks, and persistently behind—matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive worries and repeated awakenings, consistent with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive sadness most of the time, consistent with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes (3-4 times) triggered by minor stressors, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS item scores total 24, well above the 14-point cutoff for probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. The pattern mirrors five or more <med>DSM-5</med> criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, significant self-blame, psychomotor agitation/retardation (feeling "heavy"), fatigue and feeling overwhelmed, sleep disturbance, and recurrent tearful episodes. Co-occurring <med>anxiety symptoms</med> and panic-like episodes are also prominent. The patient denies suicidal ideation (Item 10 = 0). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within one week for full diagnostic evaluation and treatment planning
2. Consider evidence-based therapies such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> tailored for postpartum depression
3. Discuss possible <med>antidepressant medication</med> benefits and risks, especially if breastfeeding
4. Involve supportive family or friends to share night-time baby care so you can obtain 4-5 hour stretches of sleep
5. Provide immediate contact numbers for local crisis lines or <med>Postpartum Support International</med> (1-800-944-4773) for 24-hour support
6. Schedule follow-up re-screen in two weeks to monitor symptom trajectory and safety
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Source: 10-item self-report (Edinburgh format) – 3 wk postpartum

Symptoms & Observations  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, frequent tearfulness  
- Marked guilt/self-blame re infant care  
- Chronic, often unprovoked, anxiety with panic surges; somatic tension  
- Sleep initiation/maintenance impaired by rumination, not solely infant demands  
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to “keep up,” yet denies self-harm ideation  
- Maintains basic attachment to infant; no current safety concerns toward self or baby

Pattern Consistent With  
– Moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms  
– Comorbid anxiety, possible panic features  
– Functional impairment in self-care and home management

Risk Factors Flagged  
✓ Daily crying, pervasive sadness  
✓ Loss of pleasure/enjoyment  
✓ Excessive guilt / cognitive distortions  
✓ Anxiety & panic interfering with rest  
✓ Sleep disruption linked to mood, not only environmental demands  
✓ Denies suicidal or infanticidal ideation

Screening Impression  
Responses meet threshold for probable major postpartum depression with co-occurring anxiety; further clinical evaluation (diagnostic interview, suicide risk reassessment, and treatment planning) recommended within 1 week.
